characters: Ayamga: an eight-year-old Ghanaian boy with short hair wearing an orange T-shirt and navy shorts.
Mama Kuuire: his calm, caring mother wearing a turquoise-and-gold patterned wrapper cloth and matching headwrap.
The health worker: a friendly Ghanaian community nurse in a crisp clean teal-and-white clinic uniform.

narrationPlan.voice: A tired boy’s voice for Ayamga; a calm mother’s voice for Mama Kuuire
narrationPlan.pace: Calm and caring, never frightening (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

culturalNotes: Water stored in open pots can pick up germs, and diarrhoea is a common illness in many places. The story follows the NaCCA Science standard on illnesses spread by water (B2.5.2.1.2).
The story says to mix ORS with clean safe water and to go to a clinic. It does not give doses. Health workers should review this page.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check with a health worker that the advice (ORS, small sips, clinic visit, safe water, handwashing with soap) matches Ghana Health Service guidance.
Check that the story is calm and does not frighten children.

teacherGuide.overview: A boy gets a bad tummy after drinking unsafe water. Children learn that germs spread through unsafe water, that ORS and a health worker help, and how to keep water safe. Based on NaCCA Science standards on illnesses spread by water.
learningGoals: Say how unsafe water can make people sick.
Name two ways to keep water safe.
Say what to do when someone has a bad tummy.

beforeReading: Ask: where does your drinking water come from? How do you keep it?
whileReading: Pause on page 5 and list the safe-water rules.
afterReading: Make a poster: cover, clean cup, wash hands.
discussion: Why is it important to tell an adult when your tummy hurts?
How can the whole community keep water safe?
reflection: What will you do the next time you are very thirsty?

support: Use pictures of a covered pot and an open pot.
stretch: Say why ORS is mixed only with clean, safe water.

culturalNotes: Water stored in open pots can pick up germs, and diarrhoea is a common illness in many places. The story follows the NaCCA Science standard on illnesses spread by water (B2.5.2.1.2).
The story says to mix ORS with clean safe water and to go to a clinic. It does not give doses. Health workers should review this page.
localiseThis: Use the water sources in your community. Children must never boil water or handle hot containers.
Follow local health guidance on water treatment.

factCheck.explanation: Have a health worker confirm the ORS and clinic advice.
